name: The Steel Man
statement: Before you refute an argument, rebuild it into the strongest version its holder could give.
statementAccent: rebuild it into the strongest version its holder could give
meaning: A steel man argument, or steelmanning, is the practice of addressing the strongest possible form of an opponent's argument, even a form stronger than the one they actually presented, rather than a weakened version. It is the deliberate opposite of the straw man, the fallacy of attacking a distorted, feeble caricature of a position. To steelman is to reconstruct the other side's case in its most defensible, most persuasive shape, repairing obvious slips and supplying the best available support, and only then to respond to it. The term is a self-conscious play on straw man: steel is strong where straw is weak. It applies the rhetorical principle of charity to argument, and it is prized as a virtue of good-faith debate. If you can defeat the strongest version of a view, your refutation is far more convincing than if you had merely knocked down a caricature; and if you cannot, you have learned something worth knowing.
mechanism: Steelmanning inverts the move that makes the straw man fallacious. Where the straw man substitutes a weak, misrepresented version of an argument that is easy to knock down, the steel man does the reverse: it strengthens the argument, removing flawed assumptions that could be cheaply refuted and developing the strongest points that counter one's own position, before mounting a response. The idea is that a criticism aimed at the best form of a view is airtight in a way that a criticism of its worst form is not, and that developing counters to a steel man tends to produce a stronger argument for one's own side. The practice applies the principle of charity, reading an interlocutor in their most rational light, but many treat it as going further: charity interprets what the person actually meant, whereas steelmanning may construct an even better argument than the one given, caring more about whether the position is true than about whether it is true for the reasons its advocate offered. That extra step is both its power and the source of its main criticism.

examples.text: Rather than attacking an opponent's clumsiest phrasing, one restates their case in its strongest form and then responds to that.

examples.tag: The opposite of the straw man
examples.text: Where a straw man knocks down a caricature, a steel man strengthens the argument so the eventual refutation actually lands.
If the strongest version survives your objections, you have discovered that the position may be right, or that your own view needs work.

variants.name: Steelmanning as charity-plus
variants.text: The view that steelmanning applies and extends the principle of charity, sometimes building a better argument than the person actually gave.

variants.name: The critique of steelmanning
variants.text: The worry that improving someone's argument can misrepresent their actual position, be condescending, or dodge what they really said.

whyItMatters: Steelmanning has become a widely invoked norm of good-faith argument and critical thinking, a vivid counterpart to the straw man fallacy that everyone is warned against. Its value is both epistemic and ethical. Epistemically, engaging the strongest form of an opposing view guards against confirmation bias, forces one to find better reasons, and makes any resulting refutation genuinely decisive rather than a hollow victory over a caricature. Ethically, it embodies respect for one's interlocutor and for the process of reasoning, treating disagreement as a search for the truth rather than a contest to be won by distortion. Popularised in rationalist and online discourse in the early 2010s, the term gave a memorable name to a practice long implicit in the philosophical principle of charity. Even its critics, who warn that it can slide into misrepresenting what someone actually meant, testify to its influence as a touchstone for how to argue well and honestly.

working.text: restate the opponent's argument in its most defensible version, repairing weak points and adding the best available support.
aim for a version the holder would recognise and endorse, so the exercise engages their real position rather than a substitute.
direct criticism at this strongest form, so that a successful refutation is decisive and a failed one teaches you something.

limits: Steelmanning is a norm of good argument, not an unqualified good, and it carries a real tension. By constructing a version stronger than the one actually presented, it can drift into misrepresenting the person's genuine position, attributing to them reasoning they never offered, which is a distortion in the opposite direction from the straw man. Critics, including the statistician Andrew Gelman, argue that bending over backward to one viewpoint can implicitly dismiss others, that steelmanning can be condescending, and that it can be used to avoid engaging with what someone really said. Its relation to the principle of charity is close but debated, since charity aims at fidelity to what was meant while steelmanning may go beyond it. The term is modern and informal, popularised online in the 2010s, and its exact coinage is uncertain. So steelmanning is a valuable discipline for honest debate, best used to strengthen without silently substituting a different argument for the one a person actually holds.
misreadings: Steelmanning does not mean agreeing with an opponent or conceding their case; it means engaging its strongest form before judging it, and one can steelman a view and still reject it. It is not merely restating an argument politely, but reconstructing it at its most defensible. And it is not automatically virtuous, since improving on what someone said can misrepresent what they actually meant, so treating steelmanning as endorsement, or as a licence to replace a person's argument with a better one they never made, misreads a practice meant to make criticism fair and decisive rather than to distort or to dodge.
origin: A modern, informal term coined as the inverse of straw man and popularised in rationalist and online discourse in the early 2010s (dated to around 2011, with LessWrong among its early homes); an application of the older philosophical principle of charity.

sources.text: Straw man, Wikipedia (Steelmanning section). — the steel man as the opposite of the straw man, defined as applying the rhetorical principle of charity by addressing the strongest form of the other person's argument, and the rationale that countering the strongest form yields a stronger position.

steelman, Wiktionary. — the definition and etymology of steelman as a deliberate inverse of straw man, an improvement of a position that is harder to defeat than the one originally stated, with a 2011 origin noted.
